1.title: A Roll Read From Adam
1.context: Chronicles was written for Judah after the return from Babylonian exile. Its opening genealogy runs from Adam through the nations of Genesis to Abraham, grounding Israel's place in the whole human story.
1.question: What does it mean to you that the Bible keeps careful records of ordinary generations, not only famous people?

1.title: The Line That Outlived Exile
1.context: Chapter 3 lists David's descendants through the kings of Judah and past the exile itself, ending with the family of Zerubbabel, who led the first return and rebuilt the altar in Jerusalem.
1.question: Where in your own family's story can you trace God's faithfulness surviving a hard season?

1.title: Jabez in the List
1.context: Jabez appears nowhere else in the Bible. His name sounds like the Hebrew word for pain, and his short prayer, folded into Judah's genealogy, became one of the most quoted prayers in Scripture.
1.question: What would you ask God to change about the story your name or your past seems to tell?

1.title: The Birthright and the Battle Prayer
1.context: Reuben lost the firstborn's birthright after his sin against his father (Genesis 35:22; 49:3-4). The double portion went to Joseph's sons, while the royal line came through Judah.
1.question: The eastern tribes won when they cried out and trusted. What battle in your life needs prayer more than it needs more strength?

1.title: Singers' Ancestry and the First to Resettle
1.context: The singers Heman, Asaph, and Ethan are traced to Levi like the priests, giving the temple musicians a pedigree of their own. Chapter 9 lists the first families to resettle Jerusalem after the exile.
1.question: What work in God's house is so ordinary that it needs people willing to be named and counted for it?

2.title: The Verdict on Saul
2.context: Saul's death is told in full in 1 Samuel 31. Chronicles adds this closing verdict, explaining the fall in terms of unfaithfulness and a failure to inquire of the LORD, themes the whole book will repeat.
2.question: What is the difference between asking God for guidance and asking Him to bless a decision already made?

2.title: The Men Who Came to David
2.context: The lists of David's supporters include warriors from Saul's own tribe of Benjamin and Gadites who crossed the flooded Jordan. Issachar's men are praised not for fighting skill but for understanding the times.
2.question: Who in your life understands the times and helps you know what to do? What would it take to become that person for someone else?

2.title: We Did Not Consult Him
2.context: The ark's first journey and Uzzah's death are told in 2 Samuel 6. The Law required the ark to be carried by Levites with poles (Numbers 4:15; 7:9), which is the proper order David says was skipped.
2.question: When something goes wrong, how do you decide whether the fault is in the circumstances or in the order you skipped?

2.title: Carried on Shoulders, With Singing
2.context: Chenaniah directed the music because of his skill. David's dancing before the ark and Michal's contempt are also in 2 Samuel 6; Chronicles keeps her one verse and moves on to the worship David establishes.
2.question: What changes when worship is treated as skilled, prepared work rather than whatever happens on the day?

2.title: The Song and the Standing Ministry
2.context: David's thanksgiving song weaves together parts of Psalms 105, 96, and 106. Asaph and his brothers were left at the ark for daily ministry while Zadok served at the tabernacle in Gibeon, so worship ran in two places at once.
2.question: What daily, unglamorous faithfulness in your life is quietly doing the work of a whole ministry?

3.title: The Wars, and What Chronicles Passes By
3.context: Chapters 18 to 20 summarize David's wars, also told in 2 Samuel 8 and 10. At the spring campaign against Rabbah, 2 Samuel 11 sets David's sin with Bathsheba; Chronicles, focused on the temple and the throne, does not retell it.
3.question: Why do you think the same life can be told honestly in more than one way, with different stories brought forward?

3.title: Satan Rose Up Against Israel
3.context: Second Samuel 24:1 says the LORD's anger incited David to the census; Chronicles says Satan did. The two accounts stand side by side in Scripture without either being rewritten, and readers have weighed them together ever since.
3.question: When have you felt pushed toward a decision you already suspected was wrong? What did you do with the warning?

3.title: Let Me Fall Into the Hand of the LORD
3.context: Gad the seer had confronted David before (1 Samuel 22) and would write part of his history (1 Chronicles 29:29). David's choice of punishment trusts God's mercy more than human mercy.
3.question: What does David's choice teach about the difference between fearing consequences and trusting a Person?

3.title: Offerings That Cost Me Nothing
3.context: Ornan (called Araunah in 2 Samuel 24) was a Jebusite, from the people who held Jerusalem before David. David's refusal of a free altar became a lasting picture of worship that costs the worshiper something.
3.question: What would worship that costs you something real look like in your life this week?

3.title: Here Shall Be the House
3.context: Second Chronicles 3:1 identifies this site as Mount Moriah, the mountain of Abraham's offering in Genesis 22. The temple of Solomon, and later the temple mount in Jerusalem, stood on this ground.
3.question: Where has God turned a place of pain or failure in your life into a place where you now meet Him?

4.title: A Man of Rest
4.context: Solomon's name is related to the Hebrew word shalom, peace. Chronicles alone records this explanation of why the warrior father would not build the temple and the son of rest would.
4.question: Is there a good work you are meant to prepare for rather than complete? How do you handle that assignment?

4.title: Preparations Past Counting
4.context: A talent was roughly 34 kilograms, so the gold and silver figures here are enormous by any ancient standard. Whether read as exact treasury records or royal scale, the point is David's total commitment of his wealth to the project.
4.question: What are you stockpiling, money, skill, time, that is really meant for a purpose beyond yourself?

4.title: The Levites Organized
4.context: With the ark settled in Jerusalem, Levites no longer carried the tabernacle, so David redefined their work around the permanent house: assisting the priests, purifying, baking the showbread, and praise morning and evening.
4.question: When God settles one season of your life, what new form does faithfulness take in the next one?

4.title: Courses of Priests and Singers
4.context: The twenty-four priestly courses organized here were still serving in the New Testament: Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, belonged to the course of Abijah (Luke 1:5). The musicians' prophesying means music that carried God's word, not only melody.
4.question: What does it do to a community when even its music is organized as ministry rather than entertainment?

4.title: Gates, Treasuries, and the Unfinished Count
4.context: Chapter 27 lists the kingdom's administration, from monthly army divisions to overseers of vineyards and olive groves. Its note about Joab's unfinished census closes the shadow of chapter 21 over David's preparations.
4.question: David's first census trusted numbers; these chapters trust assigned people. Where do you see that difference in your own work?

5.title: The King Stands and Rehearses the Choice
5.context: David's assembly gathers every layer of Israel's leadership. His rehearsal of God's choosing, of Judah, of his father's house, of himself, of Solomon, echoes the pattern of election running through Genesis.
5.question: How does remembering that you were chosen for your place, rather than entitled to it, change the way you hold it?

5.title: The Charge and the Written Plan
5.context: David presents the temple plan as received in writing from the LORD, language that recalls Moses receiving the tabernacle pattern on the mountain (Exodus 25:9, 40). The weights of every vessel were specified in advance.
5.question: David tells Solomon that God searches every heart and understands every thought. Is that a comfort to you, a warning, or both?

5.title: The King's Own Treasure
5.context: Ophir was a distant source of gold, probably reached by sea trade. David separates what the crown had provided from his personal fortune, and gives the personal fortune publicly, before asking anyone else to give.
5.question: What is the difference between leading a cause with your position and leading it with your own resources first?

5.title: Willing Hearts and the Great Prayer
5.context: The gold coin called a daric was a Persian-era coin, natural for the Chronicler's own day. David's prayer here is one of the great doxologies of the Old Testament and shaped Jewish and Christian prayer for centuries.
5.question: David says everything given came from God's hand in the first place. How does that change what generosity feels like?

5.title: The Throne of the LORD
5.context: No other king is said to sit on the throne of the LORD. The Chronicler's closing note names his sources, the records of Samuel, Nathan, and Gad, an ancient historian's bibliography.
5.question: What would it mean to treat your responsibilities as a throne that belongs to God rather than to you?

6.title: One Hill, Three Stories
6.context: Solomon's wisdom request at Gibeon is told in 1 Kings 3. Second Chronicles 3:1 ties the temple site to Mount Moriah (Genesis 22) and to David's threshing floor (1 Chronicles 21), joining three stories on one hill.
6.question: What places in your life carry more than one layer of God's dealing with you?

6.title: Bronze, Gold, and the King's Treasures
6.context: The building account parallels 1 Kings 6 and 7, with some measurements differing between the books, such as the capacity of the great Sea. Chronicles emphasizes the gold, the ten lampstands and tables, and David's dedicated treasures finally coming indoors.
6.question: David's stored treasures waited years for their use. What have you set aside that is still waiting for its moment?

6.title: With One Voice
6.context: The refrain 'For He is good; His loving devotion endures forever' runs through Chronicles and the Psalms (see Psalm 136). The cloud that stops the priests recalls the glory filling the tabernacle in Exodus 40.
6.question: When have you experienced a room full of people genuinely of one voice in worship? What made it possible?

6.title: The Prayer and the Fire
6.context: Solomon's dedication prayer also stands in 1 Kings 8. Fire falling on the sacrifice answers at other great moments too: Leviticus 9, Judges 6, 1 Kings 18, and David's altar in 1 Chronicles 21.
6.question: Solomon prays most for people who will sin and turn back. What does that tell you about what the temple was for?

6.title: If My People Humble Themselves
6.context: Second Chronicles 7:14 was spoken to Solomon about Israel and the land, in a night vision after the dedication. The Queen of Sheba's visit and Solomon's wealth fill chapter 9; his fall into idolatry, told in 1 Kings 11, is not retold in Chronicles.
6.question: The promise joins humbling, praying, seeking, and turning together. Which of the four comes hardest for you?

7.title: The Turn of Events Was From God
7.context: The split of the kingdom is told in 1 Kings 12. Chronicles adds Shemaiah's word stopping Rehoboam's war of reunion, an early sign that this book measures kings by whether they listen to prophets.
7.question: Rehoboam ignored the elders but obeyed the prophet. What voices do you find easiest to hear, and which do you need to hear?

7.title: Those Who Set Their Hearts to Seek
7.context: Jeroboam's replacement priests and calf shrines (1 Kings 12-13) drove the Levites south. This migration made Jerusalem the worship center for devout people from all twelve tribes, not only Judah.
7.question: What have you left behind, or what would you leave behind, to stay where God is honestly worshiped?

7.title: The LORD Is Righteous
7.context: Shishak's invasion is confirmed outside the Bible by his campaign record carved at Karnak in Egypt, which lists towns in Israel and Judah. Solomon's gold shields, replaced here by bronze, were among the treasures he carried off.
7.question: Rehoboam's confession was four words long and it moved heaven. What keeps your own apologies longer, or later, than they need to be?

7.title: Abijah Preaches on Mount Zemaraim
7.context: Abijah's sermon rests the south's case on the Davidic covenant, which he calls a covenant of salt, salt being a sign of permanence (Numbers 18:19). First Kings remembers Abijah mainly for his sins; Chronicles preserves his sermon and his victory.
7.question: Abijah argued that worship kept God's way was itself the nation's strength. Where do you see faithfulness functioning that way?

7.title: Because They Relied on the LORD
7.context: The casualty figure given here is among the largest in the Bible. Chronicles draws its moral in one verb, relied, which becomes its standard explanation for victory all the way to Hezekiah.
7.question: What is the practical difference between relying on God and simply hoping things work out?

8.title: Help Us, O LORD Our God
8.context: Zerah the Cushite came from the south, Cush being the region below Egypt. Asa's prayer is one of the clearest statements of Chronicles' theology: God helps the powerless who rely on Him against any odds.
8.question: Asa prayed before he fought, in plain words about his weakness. What would that prayer sound like in your current situation?

8.title: The LORD Is With You When You Are With Him
8.context: Azariah son of Oded is known only from this chapter. His speech reads Israel's chaotic years in Judges as the result of being without teaching priests and the law, and Asa answers with reform and a covenant assembly.
8.question: Azariah promises that work done God's way will be rewarded. What work in front of you needs that encouragement today?

8.title: The Treaty That Worked
8.context: Hanani's picture of the LORD's eyes ranging the earth looking for hearts to strengthen is one of the best known images in Chronicles. The Aramean treaty bought real relief, which is exactly why its spiritual cost is the point.
8.question: When has a solution worked and still cost you something you did not mean to spend?

8.title: The Seer in Prison
8.context: Asa is not the first king to punish a prophet: Ahab imprisoned Micaiah (1 Kings 22), and Jeremiah would later be jailed by Zedekiah. The reflex to silence correction is one of the book's warnings about power.
8.question: Who is allowed to correct you, really? What happens inside you in the first minute after they do?

8.title: He Did Not Seek the LORD
8.context: The text does not condemn physicians; it says Asa sought them and did not seek the LORD, the reversal of his young reign. His burial honors were genuine, with a great fire of spices, as was also done for later kings.
8.question: Asa's drift happened over decades. What small habit keeps your own seeking from quietly stopping?

9.title: Teachers With the Book of the Law
9.context: No other king sends out an official teaching mission like this. The team joined civil officials, Levites, and priests, suggesting the law was taught as the constitution of the whole national life, not only as religion.
9.question: Jehoshaphat taught before he demanded. Where in your responsibilities would teaching first change the outcome?

9.title: Is There Not Still a Prophet?
9.context: The Ramoth-gilead campaign and Micaiah's vision are told in 1 Kings 22. Jehoshaphat's instinct to ask for one more voice, when four hundred agree, is the moment that defines him in the chapter.
9.question: When everyone around you agrees, what makes you ask for the one more voice, and what makes you afraid to?

9.title: Jehoshaphat Cried Out
9.context: Ahab's disguise and death by a randomly drawn bow are told in 1 Kings 22. Chronicles keeps the focus on the allied king who should not have been there, and the cry that brought him home.
9.question: Jehoshaphat was rescued from a battle he chose against a prophet's warning. How do you receive mercy that arrives inside your own mistake?

9.title: Should You Help the Wicked?
9.context: Jehu son of Hanani also confronted Baasha (1 Kings 16), and his father Hanani was the seer Asa imprisoned. Jehoshaphat's answer to rebuke is a personal ride through his kingdom turning people back to God.
9.question: Jehu's rebuke names both the sin and the good in the same man. How does correction land differently when it does both?

9.title: Not Judging for Man, but for the LORD
9.context: The two-chief structure in Jerusalem, priest for matters of the LORD and a prince for matters of the king, with Levites as officers, is an early picture of a court system with an appeal level above local judges.
9.question: Where do you exercise judgment over others, at work or at home, and what would judging 'for the LORD' change there?

10.title: Our Eyes Are Upon You
10.context: Jehoshaphat's prayer deliberately echoes Solomon's dedication prayer (2 Chronicles 6), claiming its promises for a new crisis. Abraham is called God's friend here, as also in Isaiah 41:8 and James 2:23.
10.question: 'We do not know what to do' is an unusual thing for a leader to say out loud. What does it make possible when one does?

10.title: The Battle Does Not Belong to You
10.context: Jahaziel was a Levite of Asaph's line, one of the temple singers, so the answer to the king's prayer comes through the worship staff rather than a court prophet. His words echo Moses at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:13-14).
10.question: Standing firm is the whole assignment in this battle. What does standing firm look like when you are used to fixing things?

10.title: Singers at the Head of the Army
10.context: The refrain the choir sings is the temple refrain of 2 Chronicles 5 and 7. The enemy coalition's self-destruction recalls Gideon's battle in Judges 7, where confusion did the fighting.
10.question: The singing began before anyone saw a result. What would praise in advance look like in the situation you are facing?

10.title: The Valley of Beracah
10.context: Beracah means blessing or praise. Naming places after God's acts was an old Israelite habit, from Bethel in Genesis to Ebenezer in 1 Samuel 7.
10.question: What place or date in your life deserves a Beracah name, a marker that says God fought there?

10.title: The Wrecked Ships
10.context: The Tarshish fleet venture repeats Jehoshaphat's one persistent error, alliance with the northern kings, this time with Ahab's son Ahaziah. Eliezer's prophecy and the wreck close the reign on its unresolved note.
10.question: Why do you think a person can learn a lesson in a crisis and still repeat the mistake in calm weather?

11.title: A Letter From Elijah
11.context: Elijah's ministry belongs to the northern kingdom in 1 and 2 Kings, and this letter is his only recorded writing. Some readers have wondered how a letter from Elijah reached Jehoram years after Elijah was taken up; the text simply presents it as his word to the king.
11.question: The letter lists charges before it announces consequences. What does it say that the charge came in writing, impossible to unhear or misremember?

11.title: To No One's Regret
11.context: Jehoram's disease and death fulfill the letter point by point. Ahaziah's burial with respect, out of regard for his grandfather Jehoshaphat, shows the book keeping kindness and judgment in the same ledger across generations.
11.question: What kind of ending are you building toward, one people will grieve, or one they will quietly accept with relief?

11.title: The Hidden King and the Coup
11.context: The rescue and crowning of Joash are also told in 2 Kings 11. Jehoshabeath, who hid the child, was both the baby's aunt and the high priest's wife, and the boy was raised inside the temple itself for six years.
11.question: Jehoiada waited six years for the right moment. What are you protecting now that is not yet ready to be brought out?

11.title: The Chest, the Repair, and the Priest's Burial
11.context: The temple repair under Joash is also told in 2 Kings 12, where the chest stands in the account. Jehoiada's burial among the kings is unique in the Bible for a priest, earned by a lifetime the text summarizes as good done for God and His temple.
11.question: Jehoiada's honors came at the end of a hundred and thirty years of steady good. What steady good is your life quietly accumulating?

11.title: May the LORD See This
11.context: Zechariah son of Jehoiada is remembered in the New Testament: Jesus names him among the righteous murdered between Abel and the prophets (Matthew 23:35), joining the first martyr and this one as bookends of the Hebrew Scriptures' story.
11.question: Joash forgot a kindness that had saved his life and his throne. What kindness do you most need to remember on purpose?

12.title: The Hundred Talents
12.context: A talent of silver was a fortune; a hundred talents bought a hundred thousand soldiers. The man of God's answer treats the loss as small beside what God can give, but Amaziah still has to absorb it before the battle.
12.question: What loss might God be asking you to absorb rather than recover, trusting He can give much more than this?

12.title: Gods That Could Not Deliver
12.context: Amaziah's war with Jehoash of Israel, the broken wall of Jerusalem, and his death at Lachish are told in 2 Kings 14. Chronicles adds the Edomite gods and the silenced prophet, the two moments where the king's heart shows.
12.question: Why would a victorious king worship the gods of the army he just beat? What modern version of that logic do you recognize?

12.title: Helped Until He Became Powerful
12.context: Uzziah's war engines are the Bible's one mention of such artillery in Israel. The incense altar was restricted to Aaron's priests (Exodus 30; Numbers 16-18), and Korah's company had died over this same trespass centuries earlier.
12.question: Uzziah's fall came through strength, not weakness. Which of your strengths most needs watching?

12.title: He Was a Leper
12.context: Leprosy excluded Uzziah from the temple and from ordinary society (Leviticus 13-14). Isaiah's prophecy opens 'in the year that King Uzziah died' (Isaiah 6:1), when Isaiah saw another King in that same temple.
12.question: Jotham grew powerful by not forcing the door his father forced. What door in your life needs respect rather than pressure?

12.title: Ahaz and the Opened Hand of Oded
12.context: The captives' return is one of the Hebrew Bible's striking acts of enemy mercy, set in Jericho, the city of palms, where the freed families were handed to their brothers. Ahaz, by contrast, ends the chapter shutting the temple and multiplying altars.
12.question: Oded's rebuke was aimed at the winners. When have you seen someone with the advantage told to stop, and actually stop?

13.title: The Doors Opened
13.context: Hezekiah's first-month reforms reverse his father Ahaz point by point: doors shut are opened, vessels discarded are restored, and the covenant his father broke is the new king's stated intention.
13.question: If you had one first act to signal a new direction, as Hezekiah had the doors, what would yours be?

13.title: The Song of the LORD Began
13.context: The instruments are David's, the words David's and Asaph's, and the officers include Gad and Nathan, joining the revival to the prophets who served David. The Levites outpacing the priests in consecration is recorded without embarrassment.
13.question: The chapter ends rejoicing that God prepared everything quickly. Where have you seen long preparation suddenly become a fast work of God?

13.title: Letters From Beersheba to Dan
13.context: Beersheba to Dan was the classic phrase for the whole land, south to north. The second-month Passover had a basis in the Law for those unclean or traveling (Numbers 9:10-11), which Hezekiah extends to a nation.
13.question: The letters were mocked in most towns and welcomed in a few. How do you keep an invitation open after it has been scorned?

13.title: Hezekiah Interceded for Them
13.context: Nothing like this feast since Solomon is high praise in a book that measures everything against David and Solomon. The blessing of the priests and Levites at the close is said to reach heaven itself.
13.question: Hezekiah prayed for people who had come seeking God in the wrong condition, and God healed them. What does that tell you about how God weighs the heart against the rules?

13.title: Heaps, a Gate Speech, and a Humbled Heart
13.context: Sennacherib's invasion, the tunnel, and the deliverance are told in 2 Kings 18-20 and Isaiah 36-39. Hezekiah's tunnel bringing the Gihon spring inside the walls can still be walked in Jerusalem today, with an inscription from his workers found inside it.
13.question: Hezekiah's pride and his humbling stand in the same chapter. What helps you humble yourself before circumstances do it for you?

14.title: Manasseh Undoes His Father
14.context: Manasseh's wickedness is catalogued in 2 Kings 21 as the reason Judah's doom became certain. The Assyrian practice of leading captives with hooks is pictured on Assyrian palace reliefs of the period.
14.question: Manasseh heard the LORD speak and did not listen. What is the difference between hearing a warning and listening to it?

14.title: In His Distress He Humbled Himself
14.context: Manasseh's capture and repentance are recorded only in Chronicles, not in Kings. A later work called the Prayer of Manasseh imagines his prayer, but it is not part of the Berean Standard Bible; the text here says simply that he prayed and God received his plea.
14.question: Manasseh is the book's extreme test of its own promise. If God received his plea, what does that mean for the person you think is beyond returning?

14.title: Josiah and the Passover of Passovers
14.context: Josiah's reforms and the found Book of the Law are told in 2 Kings 22-23. Pharaoh Necho was marching to aid Assyria against Babylon when Josiah intercepted him at Megiddo, the plain that gives Armageddon its name.
14.question: Josiah's Passover outshone every king's since Samuel. What celebration of God's goodness have you let grow smaller than it should be?

14.title: Beyond Remedy
14.context: The seventy years of exile were spoken by Jeremiah (Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10). Chronicles links them to the land's Sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34-35), as if the land itself finally kept the rests Israel skipped.
14.question: The messengers were mocked for generations before the end came. Which messenger in your life deserves a second hearing?

14.title: May He Go Up
14.context: Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC and permitted subject peoples to return home and rebuild their temples. In the Hebrew ordering of the Bible, Chronicles is the last book, so the Old Testament ends on this open door, and Ezra opens with the same decree.
14.question: The whole long history ends not with the fire but with an invitation. What invitation is God leaving open at the end of your current chapter?
